newsitem.title: USA: Abolition of Massachusetts counties debated again.
newsitem.headline: Abolition of Massachusetts counties debated again.

text.p: Like a Wagnerian opera, the saga of trying to abolish county government in Massachusetts goes on and on.

House lawmakers Wednesday again dissected the issue of wiping out the county system, a level of government that has existed since the 1600s. This after the measure dominated debate in the Senate last week and the issue consumed a day of hearings before a joint committee in April.
Just months before, Middlesex County, home to Harvard University and Massachusetts Institute of Technology, defaulted on $4.5 million of notes.
At Wednesday's hearing, Sen. Richard Moore, D-Uxbridge, a supporter of the budget section abolishing counties, also endorsed his own county abolition bill that was before the committee.
"It's time to abolish county government in Massachusetts," Moore told committee members at an afternoon hearing, State House News Service reported.
While several of the state's 14 counties are in healthy financial shape, Moore said, he told the committee their fiscal deterioration is "a matter of time."

Instead of repealing them piecemeal when they face financial hardships -- Middlesex County has a $17 million debt and could be ordered into receivership -- Moore said they should all be wiped out at once.

His bill and the version in the Senate budget have a few differences. The budget has the state paying for the counties' pension liability, and Moore would have the state study the issue for five years.
Moore would also allow county treasurers to serve out their current term, and then seek reappointment to another six-year term. The Senate plan phases out the treasurers after six months.

Both plans would transfer the counties' biggest functions -- courts, jails, and registries of deeds -- to the state on July 1, and eliminate all other functions beginning July 1, 1998. Regions that wish to keep counties intact will be allowed to establish regional governments.

Many of the bill's opponents agreed that some county function would be best controlled by the state. But they maintain counties are vital to the less populated areas of the state, where services between towns are often shared.
Further, opponents stressed that such a big issue should not be addressed in the budget, where only one branch gets to fully debate the matter.

"My greatest concern is the process," said Rep. Shirley Gomes, R-South Harwich, about abolishing counties through the budget, where House members did not participate in the debate. "It's the big issue in the budget, and you only have the option to go up or down on that. Which is the more open, more deliberative process?"
